title: Gobekli Tepe
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with iHeart intro voice) discuss Göbekli Tepe, a Neolithic site in southern Turkey that appears to predate farming and settled life. They cover its discovery and excavation under Klaus Schmidt from 1994, its T-shaped limestone pillars and animal carvings, the site's possible ritual, calendar, and astronomical functions, the beer-brewing evidence, Schmidt's hunter-gatherer ritual hypothesis, the later revisions by Lee Claire's team (water cistern, landslide and earthquake damage), competing interpretations by Thomas Zimmerman and Anna Fagan, and the Graeber and Wengrow "Dawn of Everything" seasonal-gathering idea. The episode closes with a listener mail segment from CR about Ford's Rouge plant and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about concerts, a recommended movie called Triangle, and then introduce the topic of Göbekli Tepe.

segments.title: Name and the Neolithic Revolution background
segments.summary: The name Göbekli Tepe is explained as 'pot belly hill'. The hosts describe the traditional Neolithic Revolution story of settled farming in the Fertile Crescent, which Göbekli Tepe seems to upend.

segments.title: Discovery and Klaus Schmidt's excavation
segments.summary: The 1960s survey mistook limestone slabs for medieval gravestones. Excavation under Klaus Schmidt beginning in 1994 revealed a Neolithic site dated to about 11,600 years ago.

segments.title: Site layout, size, and age levels
segments.summary: The mound is about fifty feet tall and twenty-two acres, located in the Germuş mountains. Layers were dug top down, with the most recent use around ten thousand years ago and the oldest about eleven thousand six hundred years ago.

segments.title: Pillars and enclosures
segments.summary: Upper-level limestone pillars with lion etchings give way to larger pillars below, up to about sixteen to eighteen feet tall and around ten tons. At least twenty circular enclosures have arrangements that may form a triangle, possibly an observatory.

segments.title: Construction effort and debate over moving stones
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the coordination needed to quarry and raise the pillars and the debate over how many people it took, including Edward Banning's view that about twenty crew could do it.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Animal carvings and clan enclosures
segments.summary: Pictograms of wild animals such as birds, gazelles, foxes and scorpions are carved on the pillars. Some enclosures seem dedicated to one animal, possibly representing clans, and the largest enclosure D mixes many animals.

segments.title: T-shaped pillars, rituals, beer, and proto-writing
segments.summary: The T-shaped pillars represent the head viewed from the side. Ritual use is suggested by ceremonial masks and beer brewing vats. Repeated symbols may be proto-writing, and Martin Sweatman's reading of pillar markings as a calendar tied to a possible comet impact is described.

segments.title: Diet and evidence of hunter-gatherers
segments.summary: Animal bones show mostly gazelle with sheep, deer, boar, and birds. Plant remains and the lack of domesticated animal bones suggest the builders were still hunter-gatherers, and the hosts connect this to beer preceding farming.

segments.title: Lack of permanent settlement evidence
segments.summary: No trash mounds, hearths, homes, or water source were found at first, and the carvings include death symbolism such as a headless human figure.

segments.title: Klaus Schmidt's original hypothesis
segments.summary: Schmidt proposed that Göbekli Tepe was a ritual site used by hunter-gatherers who gathered periodically to feast, drink, build, and fill enclosures with rubble, and that this gathering drew people into farming. The hosts joke about the chicken-or-egg question.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with a teaser about new evidence.

segments.title: Post-Schmidt excavation and revised hypothesis
segments.summary: Lee Claire of the German Archaeological Institute built a canopy and dug deeper, finding a thirty-foot cistern and evidence supporting permanent occupation. Earthquake and landslide damage suggests rebuilding rather than rubble filling. Shout-out to journalist Andrew Curry.

segments.title: Competing interpretations and excavation status
segments.summary: Lee Claire's team suggests a backlash against farming. Thomas Zimmerman sees a male-dominated conservative group with violent initiation themes. The hosts discuss how much of the site remains unexcavated, with most of it still buried.

segments.title: Dawn of Everything and seasonal hunter-gatherers
segments.summary: Graeber and Wengrow's book The Dawn of Everything argues for diverse non-agricultural societies. They suggest Göbekli Tepe was a seasonal gathering place for bands in times of plenty.

segments.title: Holiday seasons as ancient tradition and song joke
segments.summary: The hosts link the gathering to modern holiday seasons. Chuck sings a snippet of 'Welcome to the Boomtown' as a joke.

segments.title: Anna Fagan's life and death symbolism interpretation
segments.summary: Anna Fagan from the University of Melbourne interprets the death and animal imagery as symbolizing life, death, and regeneration, and the hosts jokingly propose calling it the Welcome to the Boomtown theory.

segments.title: Listener mail from CR about Ford Rouge plant
segments.summary: A listener named CR shares extra facts about the Ford Motor Company's Rouge River plant and Henry Ford's prohibition views, and the hosts thank them.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and invite extra-info emails; production credit given.
